background.definition: Autism spectrum disorders (ASDs) are a group of life-long neurodevelopmental disorders that initially manifest in early childhood. Children with autism have core deficits in reciprocal social interactions, verbal and nonverbal communication, and restricted and repetitive patterns of behavior or interest. This group of disorders includes autistic disorder (classical autism), Asperger's disorder, and pervasive developmental disorder not otherwise specified (PDD-NOS).

list.listitem: Based on recent CDC surveillance data, there is an increasing prevalence of ASD from 1 in every 150 children in the year 2000, to 1 in 59 in the year 2014.
Males are affected more than females with a ratio of 3:1 to 6:1.

Prevalence estimates have markedly increased over the last two decades. It is unclear how much this represents a true increase in the incidence of ASDs. Broadened diagnostic criteria, heightened awareness, and diagnostic substitution, whereby children receiving special education have been reclassified as "autistic," also need to be considered as contributing factors.
Anxiety disorders, ADHD and oppositional defiant disorder are common in children with ASD.
Up to 70% children with ASD have at least one psychiatric comorbidity, while up to 40% have two or more psychiatric comorbidities.

Autism spectrum disorders are thought to be complex heritable disorders that involve the interplay of multiple genes and environmental factors. Large genetic component exists for developing ASD. In one study, pairwise ASD concordance was 31% for dizygotic twins and 88% for monozygotic twins.
Autism may be associated with both advanced maternal and paternal age.

In less than 10% of cases, autism may be associated with distinct medical conditions, most notably fragile X syndrome, tuberous sclerosis, fetal alcohol syndrome, Angelman syndrome, and untreated phenylketonuria.

There is no consistent relation between low birth weight, intrauterine growth restriction, or other perinatal factors and autism. The increased risk of autistic disorders related to preterm birth that is seen in some studies may be mediated by pregnancy and neonatal complications that occur more commonly among preterm infants.
Current evidence does not support a causal relation between MMR or thimerosal-containing vaccines and autism.
A cohort study in Denmark with over 1 million children found no association with the likelihood of childhood disorders including autism with exposure to vaccines containing aluminum.
A study of 39,725 infants exposed to influenza vaccine in utero, including 13,845 in the first trimester, found no association with autism during a mean 6.7 years of follow-up.

In vitro fertilization (IVF) does not increase the overall risk for autism; however, when limited to IVF procedures associated with intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI) risk for autistic disorders among offspring was increased. However, a national cohort study in Denmark identified 57,964 children conceived using assisted reproductive technologies (ART) and compared them with other children up to 7 years of age. ART included IVF in 46% and intracytoplasmic sperm injection in 24%; ART parents were older and more highly educated, on average. The rate of low birth weight was higher in the ART group (17.5% vs 5.1%), as was prematurity (15.8% vs 5.1%). After controlling for low birth weight and prematurity, associations between ART and neurodevelopmental disorders including autism were no longer significant. The authors concluded that the association between ART and neurodevelopmental disorders in early childhood is mediated by low birth weight and prematurity.

A significant association exists between prenatal exposure to valproate (defined as exposure from 30 days before the estimated day of conception to the day of birth) and an increased risk of autism spectrum disorders (4.42% with exposure vs. 1.53% without exposure; NNH 35). No increased risk was noted for prenatal exposure to oxcarbazepine, lamotrigine, clonazepam, or carbamazepine.
The association with valproate was also seen in a large registry study (10.5% with valproate vs 4.2% unexposed). No significant association was seen with topiramate or lamotrigine.
There is also an increased risk among children of mothers with gestational diabetes before 26 weeks (HR 1.39; 95% CI 1.1-1.7).
There is no association between labor induction and autism spectrum disorder.
A large Swedish retrospective cohort study found no association between first trimester maternal antidepressant use and autism spectrum disorder.
There is no association between acetaminophen use during pregnancy and autism, ADHD or intellectual disability.
A systematic review of individual patient data found a possible association between low materal levels of free thyroxine and autism.
There is no association between use of epidural anesthesia and autism spectrum disorder based on a large Danish cohort study.
In a meta-analysis of 17 observational studies with 534,445 participants, prenatal exposure to cannabis was not associated with an increased incidence of autism.

Leading candidate genes for ASDs include loci on chromosomes 2, 3, 7, 15, 17, and chromosome X. One study found changes in copy number of microcephalin 1 as a susceptibility factor for ASD in the distal short arm of chromosome 8 in four patients with ASD.

Tissue studies suggest maturational and organizational defects in the brains of people with autism likely have their origin in the prenatal period of development. Abnormalities include reduced numbers of Purkinje cells in the cerebellum and abnormal maturation of the forebrain limbic system. In addition, corpus callosum reductions are present in patients with autism supporting the aberrant connectivity hypothesis.

Maternal history of rheumatoid arthritis or celiac disease

list.listitem: The AAP recommends screening all children at 18 and 24 months of age with an ASD specific screening tool. C

The USPSTF concluded that there was insufficient evidence regarding the benefits and harms of screening for ASD in otherwise asymptomatic children 18 to 30 months of age. Clinical judgment should be used, for example considering screening when parents or caregivers may not be able to reliably provide information about a child's behavior or may be less likely to notice behavioral issues. B

While the CHAT and modified CHAT (M-CHAT) both have good specificity and can be used to screen in the office setting, the modified version has better sensitivity and is less likely to miss high-functioning children with ASD (). C

Despite lack of systematic evidence that screening improves outcomes, early screening and diagnosis of children with ASDs is thought to be important because the best outcomes have been demonstrated in children who receive at least 2 years of intensive behavioral intervention during the preschool years.
The American Academy of Pediatrics now recommends screening all children for autism at 18 and 24 months of age with an ASD specific screening tool.
However, the USPSTF found insufficient evidence to recommend screening, as existing treatment trials were small, heterogeneous, and enrolled only non-screen detected (and very symptomatic) children.

The Modified Checklist for Autism in Toddlers with Follow-up (M-CHAT/F) is a simple and freely available screening instrument for autism spectrum disorders. An online version is available for no cost.

summarizes the results of two large US studies of the M-CHAT. The positive predictive value ranged from 30% to 47% depending on how it was calculated; many of the patients who screened positive but were not diagnosed with autism had other potentially treatable developmental or language delays.

A study of 25,999 children screened using M-CHAT with follow-up at 16 to 26 months. A the initial screening, 9.1% of kids screened positive, but 95% were no longer considered to have ASD and at 4 years of age the final prevalence of ASD was only 2.2%. The positive predictive value was only 15%, so 85% of children initially screening positive were false alarms.
Refer children suspected of having an ASD for both educational intervention services and a comprehensive ASD evaluation simultaneously. C

Red flags for immediate evaluation include: no babbling, pointing or other gesture by 12 months, no single words by 16 months, no 2-word spontaneous (not echolalic) phrases by 24 months, and regression of language or social skills at any age. C
All children suspected of having an ASD should undergo formal audiological testing and lead screening. C
Routine laboratory tests, genetic screening, neuroimaging, and EEG are not indicated in most patients. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Rapid loss of language and motor hand skills, predominantly seen in girls
Normal development through age 2, followed by loss of language, social, play skills
Can coexist with autism; in MR alone social skills appropriate for developmental age
Primary deficit in language or communication; social skills are well preserved
Child can speak in some situations, but mute in others
Relatively normal development followed by onset of hallucinations and delusions
Unusual interests or behaviors, but social skills and language skills are preserved

list.listitem: Parental concerns and history should be targeted towards deficits in the three core areas of autism: social skills, communication, and restricted patterns of behavior, interests, and activities (see ). Any red flags or regression should prompt an immediate referral for comprehensive ASD evaluation, regardless of screening test results.

Deficits in reciprocal social interactions and joint attention, whereby an infant shows enjoyment in sharing an object or event with another person by looking back and forth, are two of the most specific deficits in young children with ASDs.

Most children who are diagnosed with Autistic Disorder and PDD present with speech delay, but other abnormalities of verbal and preverbal communication are also common, including lack of appropriate gestures and gaze and persistent echolalia.

Children with Asperger's syndrome may escape early detection due to relatively normal speech development. Such children may not be diagnosed until early school age, when pragmatic deficits in speech and inability to initiate and maintain conversations with other children become more evident.
There is no single diagnostic test for autism, and universal expanded laboratory testing and EEGs are not recommended.
Genetic and metabolic testing are indicated only under certain circumstances (see ). Positive results are unlikely in children with high functioning autism or PDD-NOS.
Indications for EEG include clinical seizures and suspicion of subclinical seizure activity. EEGs should be considered in children who demonstrate clear regression of language milestones.

There is no evidence to support routine neuroimaging or other tests such as hair analysis, celiac antibodies, urinary peptides, tests for heavy metals, thyroid function tests, and testing for food, yeast, and mold allergies in children with ASDs.
No relevant clinical decision rules found.

In addition to formal screening at 18 and 24 months of age, ongoing developmental surveillance should be performed at all well child care visits. If an ASD is suspected, the child should be referred to early intervention if under age 3, or to the special education department of the local school district if age 3 or above.
Simultaneously, refer child for a comprehensive, multidisciplinary ASD evaluation that includes IQ testing and a formal evaluation of adaptive behavior (see algorithm in ).
All children suspected of having autism should have a formal audiological evaluation to rule out hearing loss and lead testing, especially in those with a history of pica.
All children with ASD should receive speech therapy and a minimum of 25 hours per week of intensive behavioral and educational intervention. C
Early intensive behavioral interventions results in improved outcomes, primarily measured IQ. Interventions that train parents rather than just educate them are more effective.B
Applied behavioral analysis (ABA) therapy can be effective in improving IQ, adaptive behavior, and functional outcome of children with ASD. B

When used as adjunctive therapy, risperidone and aripiprazole can improve irritability and other behavioral symptoms. Benefit must be balanced against the lack of long-term data and adverse effects. A
There is insufficient evidence to recommend vitamin B6 and magnesium, auditory integration training, music therapy, and gluten- and casein-free diet. B

Medication should be considered as adjunctive therapy if behavioral symptoms cause significant impairment in functioning or do not respond to primary behavioral interventions. There should be ongoing quantifiable assessment of the efficacy of the medication in treating the targeted behavior.

Risperidone can improve irritability and global behavioral problems in children with autism, compared to placebo (69% vs. 12%; NNT 1.8). It can also improve social withdrawal, hyperactivity, and stereotypical behaviors. However, these results must be balanced against the small size of RCTs, the lack of long-term data, and the potential for significant side effects, including weight gain. An uncontrolled 2 year follow-up study of 84 subjects found some apparent benefits, but also higher rates of enuresis, excessive appetite and weight gain.

A Cochrane review identified 3 short-term (8-week) placebo-controlled trials of aripiprazole, and concluded that it was effective at improving behaviors associated with ASD including irritability and hyperactivity. Adverse effects included weight gain, sedation, and tremor. A systematic review of 5 studies concluded that aripiprazole was similarly safe and effective to risperidone.

SSRIs can improve repetitive behaviors, irritability, depressive symptoms, anxiety, aggression and certain aspects of social interaction. These results are based primarily on open-label studies. In one 12-week RCT of citalopram in children and adolescents with ASD, there was no significant difference in repetitive behavior.

A Cochrane review concluded that there is no evidence of a positive effect of SSRI's in children with ASDs and "emerging evidence of harm," and there is insufficient evidence on the effectiveness of SSRIs in adults.

A study of 146 children and adolescents 7 to 18 years of age with ASD and obsessive compulsive symptoms randomized them fluoxetine or placebo. At 16 weeks, behavioral scores were lower in the treatment group, but the difference was of borderline clinical significance.

Based on recent controlled trials, methylphenidate may improve hyperactivity, impulsivity, and inattention in children with ASDs. However, the response rate is lower than in children with isolated ADHD, and adverse effects are frequent, including exacerbation of core autistic symptoms.

Centrally-acting alpha-agonists such as clonidine and guanfacine may reduce hyperarousal symptoms, irritability, outbursts, and impulsivity in children with ASDs. However, these drugs have a narrow therapeutic window and can produce serious adverse effects, including sedation, dry mouth, hypotension, and electrocardiographic abnormalities.
A well designed RCT with 290 participants with autism spectrum disorder found no benefit of intranasal oxytocin.
There is insufficient evidence to recommend the use of combined vitamin B6 and magnesium therapy.

A small randomized trial (n = 42) found that over 20 weeks, patients with autism who were given placebo and vitamin D 2000 IU daily, all improved somewhat with a somewhat greater (non-significant) improvement in the placebo group.
There is insufficient evidence to recommend the use of omega-3 fatty acids or melatonin.
Intravenous secretin is not effective as a treatment for autism.

There is insufficient systematic evidence to recommend auditory integration training (AIT) or other alternative therapies, including chelation therapy, craniosacral manipulation, facilitated communication, antifungal and probiotic agents, intravenous immunoglobulin and accupuncture.

Children with ASDs should receive speech therapy under the direction of a speech-language pathologist. Speech therapy should be highly intensive and should stress functional communication goals in concert with other educational objectives.
In non-verbal children, augmentative modalities, including sign language and picture communication systems (PECS) can help promote verbal language skills.
Occupational therapy is frequently provided to promote development of self-care skills and academic skills such as writing, but research regarding the efficacy of OT is lacking.

In one RCT of cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) with 40 children with ASD, CBT resulted in a significantly higher proportion with a positive treatment response on the Clinical Global Impressions-Improvement scale criteria (78.5% vs. 8.7%) and improved parental reports of children's anxiety.
There is no evidence to support the use of sensory integration therapy with autistic children who exhibit abnormal sensory responses or hypersensitivity to external stimuli.
Interventions that emphasize training of parents rather than merely providing education are significantly more effective.
Children with ASDs should receive a minimum of 25 hours per week of intensive behavioral and educational intervention. Intervention should begin as soon as a preliminary diagnosis of ASD is made.

Intervention programs should be highly structured, and a substantial amount of therapy should be delivered in 1:1 and small group settings. They also should include parent training and opportunities for interaction with typically developing peers.

Educational curricula should address functional communication, social and adaptive skills, school readiness and academic skills, and reduction of maladaptive behaviors. There also should be ongoing measurement and documentation of the child's progress towards these objectives.

Applied behavior analysis (ABA) therapy, which emphasizes direct observation of behavior and functional behavior analysis, appears to be significantly more effective than "eclectic" treatment in several small studies, although results are limited by lack of random assignment to treatment groups. In these studies, preschool children who received 30 or more hours of ABA per week had significantly larger gains in IQ and adaptive behavior scores, and a larger proportion of such children were able to be fully included in regular education classrooms.

However, in a systematic review of 13 studies of ABA, the authors concluded that data are limited and results in favor of this therapy over standard care are likely due to chance; only 6 of the studies that they found were of high quality and only 4 (with 101 patients) reported data that could be pooled.

Other intervention strategies include structured teaching (TEACCH model), pivotal response training, social skills training, and developmental or relationship-focused models (e.g., "Floortime", Son-Rise, RDI, Hanen program, among others). None of these strategies has been sufficiently compared to ABA or placebo in controlled trials at this time.
Social skills training to improve social competence and enhance friendships has been demonstrated in a controlled trial of 196 individuals with autism spectrum disorders.

While a gluten-free and casein-free diet did improve autistic behavior in two small randomized studies with a total of only 35 patients, there is insufficient evidence to recommend such a diet (or other elimination diets) as part of routine clinical practice.

Music therapy can improve social interactions, verbal and nonverbal communication, initiating behavior, and social-emotional reciprocity. It may also improve parent-child relationships and social adaptation skills.
Hyperbaric oxygen therapy is not effective.
The prevalence of epilepsy in children with ASDs ranges from 11% to 39%. The risk for seizures is higher in children that have comorbid autism and mental retardation.
The onset of epilepsy in autism follows a bimodal age distribution, with the first peak before the age of 5 years and the second peak in adolescence.
Treatment is the same as for other children with epilepsy and is based on accurate diagnosis of the particular seizure type.
Mental retardation, poor functional play skills, lack of joint attention, and lack of functional speech by 5 years of age are associated with a poor prognosis. C
Performance IQ greater than 70 in childhood is associated with a more functional adult outcome. C
Most children with autistic disorder retain their diagnosis at 9 years of age, but many children improve, especially those with pervasive developmental disorder.

A minority of children have optimal outcomes and are able to function well in mainstream classrooms and with age-appropriate peers without support. However, children with ASDs who achieve "normal functioning" usually have residual signs of social awkwardness, restrictive interests, or mild stereotypies.
There are no clear criteria that accurately predict prognosis in autism, and the effect of behavioral intervention on long-term and adult outcomes has not been adequately studied.

Poorer outcomes are associated with mental retardation, poor imitation skills, poor functional play skills, lack of joint attention by 4 years of age, lack of functional speech by 5 years of age, and onset of seizures during adolescence.

In one study of 68 autistic children followed into adulthood, only 22% of the patients had a "Very Good" or "Good" outcome as adults, based on their ability to maintain employment and friendships and their ability to live reasonably independently with or without family support.

In the same study, a childhood performance IQ of at least 70 predicted a significantly better adult outcome. However, many individuals with an IQ above 70 continued to have difficulties with employment, language, and ritualistic behaviors as adults.

Since the recurrence risk for ASDs is higher compared to the general population in families with one autistic child, siblings of a child with ASD should be closely monitored for acquisition of social, communication, and play skills, and should be screened for language delays and learning difficulties in addition to being screened for ASDs.

Parents should be made aware of their rights under the federal Individuals with Disabilities Education Act (IDEA), which mandates that school districts provide a free and appropriate public education in the least restrictive environment for children with disabilities over the age of 3. Many states also have statutes that pertain to the education of children with ASDs.

Any developmental red flags? No babbling, pointing, or other gesture by 12 months No single words by 16 months No 2-word spontaneous (not echolalic) phrases by 24 months ANY loss of ANY language or social skills at ANY age
18- or 24-month visit OR Parental/caregiver concern based on historical signs (see )a
Exit algorithm, re-enter at next well child care visit
Refer for educational services Early Intervention if under age 3 Local School District if age 3 or older

Refer for comprehensive ASD evaluation, including the following: Cognitive evaluation/IQ testing Adaptive behavior evaluation Speech and language evaluation Sensorimotor/OT evaluations Neuropsychological/family assessments

Formal audiologic screening Lead testing (especially with pica) Genetic testing/DNA analysis for fragile X (only with MR, dysmorphic features, or family history of fragile X syndrome) Selective metabolic testing (only with lethargy, cyclic vomiting, and early seizures, or MR or dysmorphic features EEG (only with seizures or clear regression)

footnotes.footnote: Abbreviations: MR, mental retardation; OT, occupational therapy.
a If there is sufficient parental or caregiver concern based on multiple historical signs, child may be referred directly for educational services and ASD evaluation regardless of screen results.

feature.caption: Modified Checklist for Autism in Toddlers (M-CHAT).a
feature.feature_body:
1. Does your child enjoy being swung, bounced on your knee, etc.? Yes No
2. Does your child take an interest in other children? Yes No
3. Does your child like climbing on things, such as up stairs? Yes No
4. Does your child enjoy playing peek-a-boo/hide-and-seek? Yes No
5. Does your child ever pretend, for example, to talk on the phone or take care of dolls, or pretend other things? Yes No
6. Does your child ever use his/her index finger to point, to ask for something? Yes No
7. Does your child ever use his/her index finger to point, to indicate interest in something? Yes No
8. Can your child play properly with small toys (e.g., cars or bricks) without just mouthing, fiddling, or dropping them? Yes No
9. Does your child ever bring objects over to you (parent) to show you something? Yes No
10. Does your child look you in the eye for more than a second or two? Yes No
11. Does your child ever seem oversensitive to noise (e.g., plugging ears)? Yes No
12. Does your child smile in response to your face or your smile? Yes No
13. Does your child imitate you (e.g., if you make a face-will your child imitate it)? Yes No
14. Does your child respond to his/her name when you call? Yes No
15. If you point at a toy across the room, does your child look at it? Yes No
16. Does your child walk? Yes No
17. Does your child look at things you are looking at? Yes No
18. Does your child make unusual finger movements near his/her face? Yes No
19. Does your child try to attract your attention to his/her own activity? Yes No
20. Have you ever wondered if your child is deaf? Yes No
21. Does your child understand what people say? Yes No
22. Does your child sometimes stare at nothing or wander with no purpose? Yes No
23. Does your child look at your face to check your reaction when faced with something unfamiliar? Yes No
a Items in bold are critical items. Scoring: A child fails the checklist when two or more critical items (in bold) are failed, OR when any three items are failed. Failing responses are "No" except for questions 11, 18, 20, and 22. Adapted from Robins DL, Fein D, Barton ML, Green JA. The Modified Checklist for Autism in Toddlers. J Autism Dev Disord 2001;31:131–144. Also available at www.firstsigns.org/downloads/m-chat.pdf.

feature.caption: Clinical Signs of Autism by History.
feature.feature_body:
RED FLAGS: absolute indications for immediate evaluation
No babbling, pointing, or other gesture by 12 months
No single words by 16 months
No 2-word spontaneous (not echolalic) phrases by 24 months
ANY loss of ANY language or social skills at ANY age
Social skills deficits
Lack of joint attention
Doesn't point to or request or share objects-leads parent to object instead
Does things independently-gets things for him- or herself (“advanced motor skills”)
Aloof/in his or her own world/not interested in other children
Prefers to play alone
Lack of social smile
Lack of social referencing (less imitation of parental facial expressions)
Does not play reciprocal games such as "peek-a-boo" or "pat-a-cake"
Communication deficits
Delayed speech (most common presentation)
Rote speech without communicative intent, including persistent echolalia
Lack of communicative gestures and appropriate gaze
Selective hearing or doesn't respond to name
Cannot follow simple 1-step commands
Dissociation between "advanced" expressive skills and delayed receptive language
Delayed/absent pretend play skills, or over scripted/ritualized pretend play
Cannot initiate or sustain conversations with othersa
Formal speech limited to restricted topics, but cannot express feelingsa
Deficits in pragmatic (social) use of languagea
Deficits in prosody of speech-abnormal intonations, volume, rhythm, pitch, etc.a
Difficulty with abstract reasoning, humor, idioms, understanding feelings of othersa
Behavioral concerns (including stereotyped behaviors and Interests)
Mouths/twirls/bangs toys inappropriately
Hand flapping/finger movements/rocking/twirling/toe walking
Attends to parts of objects (i.e., spinning wheels on toy car)
Lines up objects
Plays with toys in the exact same way each time
Unusual attachments to objects-always holding blanket, hard object, etc.
Oversensitivity to certain environmental textures and sounds
Tactile defensiveness to soft objects/touch/hugging/cuddling
Difficulty with transitions between activities
Insistence on sameness (same routine, same brand of cereal, etc.)
Atypical motor development/poor coordination/deficits in praxis/clumsiness
a More common in children with Asperger's syndrome and high functioning autism/pervasive developmental disorder (PDD). Data from personal experience; Johnson CP, Myers SM; Council on Children With Disabilities. Identification and evaluation of children with autism spectrum disorders. Pediatrics 2007;120:1183–1215; and Filipek PA, Accardo PJ, Baranek GT, et al. The screening and diagnosis of autistic spectrum disorders. J Autism Dev Disord 1999;29:437–482.

feature.caption: Diagnostic Criteria for Autistic Disorder (299.00).
feature.feature_body:
A total of six (or more) items from (1), (2), and (3), with at least two from (1), and one each from (2) and (3): Qualitative impairment in social interaction, as manifested by at least two of the following: Qualitative impairments in communication as manifested by at least one of the following: Marked impairment in the use of multiple nonverbal behaviors such as eye-to-eye gaze, facial expression, body postures, and gestures to regulate social interaction Failure to develop peer relationships appropriate to developmental level A lack of spontaneous seeking to share enjoyment, interests, or achievements with other people (e.g., by a lack of showing, bringing, or pointing out objects of interest) Lack of social or emotional reciprocity Qualitative impairments in communication as manifested by at least one of the following:
Delay in, or total lack of, the development of spoken language (not accompanied by an attempt to compensate through alternative modes of communication such as gesture or mime) In individuals with adequate speech, marked impairment in the ability to initiate or sustain a conversation with others Stereotyped and repetitive use of language or idiosyncratic language Lack of varied, spontaneous make-believe play or social imitative play appropriate to developmental level
Restricted repetitive and stereotyped patterns of behavior, interests, and activities, as manifested by at least one of the following: Encompassing preoccupation with one or more stereotyped and restricted patterns of interest that is abnormal either in intensity or focus Apparently inflexible adherence to specific, nonfunctional routines or rituals Stereotyped and repetitive motor mannerisms (e.g., hand or finger flapping or twisting, or complex whole-body movements) Persistent preoccupation with parts of objects
Delays or abnormal functioning in at least one of the following areas, with onset prior to age 3 years: (1) social interaction, (2) language as used in social communication, or (3) symbolic or imaginative play. The disturbance is not better accounted for by Rett's Disorder or Childhood Disintegrative Disorder. Adapted from American Psychiatric Association. Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fourth Edition, Text Revision (DSM-IV-TR). Arlington, VA: American Psychiatric Association; 2000.

feature.caption: Diagnostic Criteria for Asperger's Disorder (299.80).
feature.feature_body:
Qualitative impairment in social interaction, as manifested by at least two of the following: Marked impairment in the use of multiple nonverbal behaviors such as eye-to-eye gaze, facial expression, body postures, and gestures to regulate social interaction Failure to develop peer relationships appropriate to developmental level A lack of spontaneous seeking to share enjoyment, interests, or achievements with other people (e.g., by a lack of showing, bringing, or pointing out objects of interest to other people) Lack of social or emotional reciprocity
Restricted repetitive and stereotyped patterns of behavior, interests, and activities, as manifested by at least one of the following: Encompassing preoccupation with one or more stereotyped and restricted patterns of interest that is abnormal either in intensity or focus Apparently inflexible adherence to specific, nonfunctional routines or rituals Stereotyped and repetitive motor mannerisms (e.g., hand or finger flapping or twisting, or complex whole-body movements) Persistent preoccupation with parts of objects
The disturbance causes clinically significant impairment in social, occupational, or other important areas of functioning. There is no clinically significant general delay in language (e.g., single words used by age 2 years, communicative phrases used by age 3 years). There is no clinically significant delay in cognitive development or in the development of age-appropriate self-help skills, adaptive behavior (other than in social interaction), and curiosity about the environment in childhood. Criteria are not met for another specific Pervasive Developmental Disorder or Schizophrenia. Adapted from American Psychiatric Association. Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fourth Edition, Text Revision (DSM-IV-TR). Arlington, VA: American Psychiatric Association; 2000.
